traditions/coptic-orthodox/summary: The church of Egypt's native Christians, tracing its origins to St Mark and led by the Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the See of St Mark. It rejected Chalcedon under Dioscorus and became the largest Christian body in the Middle East, preserving Coptic in its liturgy after Arabic became the vernacular. Its desert monasteries, revived in the twentieth century, remain spiritual centres, and a large diaspora has formed since the 1960s.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/distinctives/: Apostolic see of St Mark and the Alexandrian theological tradition
Calendar of the Martyrs beginning in AD 284
Long experience as a minority under Islamic rule
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/autho: Scripture and Holy Tradition, the teaching of the Alexandrian Fathers, and the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/salva: Salvation through faith and life in Christ, nourished by the sacraments and a life of repentance and ascetic struggle.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/sacra: Seven sacraments; baptism by triple immersion followed by chrismation and communion, including for infants.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/escha: Christ's return, the resurrection and judgment; commemoration and prayer for the departed.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/gover: Holy Synod led by the Pope of Alexandria, chosen in part by altar lot.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/worsh: Liturgies of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril; extensive fasting (over 200 days a year) and hymnody accompanied by cymbals and triangle.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/profile/canon: Old Testament including deuterocanonical books; the 27-book New Testament.
traditions/coptic-orthodox/status: Active; c. 10 million members in Egypt and the diaspora (estimates range from 5 to 15 million).
traditions/ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo/s: One of the oldest national churches, dating from the conversion of the Aksumite king Ezana under Frumentius in the fourth century. 'Tewahedo' ('made one') expresses its Miaphysite Christology. For sixteen centuries it received its head bishop from the Coptic Church, gaining its own patriarch in 1959. It preserves distinctive practices including the tabot (replica of the Ark of the Covenant) in every church, Sabbath observance, dietary laws and the broadest biblical canon in Christendom.
traditions/ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo/d: Tabot in every church, linked to the tradition that the Ark rests at Aksum
Observance of both Saturday and Sunday Sabbaths
Circumcision and Old Testament dietary practices
Ge'ez liturgy and rock-hewn churches (e.g. Lalibela)
Broadest canon (81 books), including Enoch and Jubilees
traditions/ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo/p: Scripture, Holy Tradition and the Ethiopian patristic and legal tradition (e.g. the Fetha Nagast), under the Holy Synod.
Union with Christ through faith, sacraments, fasting and prayer, leading toward the transformation of the believer.
Seven sacraments, with infant baptism and communion; marriage often blessed with the Eucharist.
Resurrection and final judgment; vivid traditions of the afterlife drawn from Enoch and other writings.
Autocephalous since 1959, led by the Patriarch of Ethiopia with a Holy Synod; a vast clergy including debtera (lay cantor-scholars).
Ge'ez liturgy with fourteen anaphoras, chant (zema) attributed to St Yared, liturgical dance and drums, and some 180–250 fast days.
The 81-book 'broader canon', including 1 Enoch, Jubilees and Meqabyan, plus church order books.
traditions/ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo/s: Active; 32.1 million in the 2007 census, now perhaps 40+ million including the diaspora.
traditions/armenian-apostolic/summary: The national church of the Armenian people, tracing its origin to the apostles Thaddeus and Bartholomew and to Gregory the Illuminator's conversion of King Tiridates III, traditionally dated 301. It formally rejected Chalcedon at the Synods of Dvin in the sixth century. Its Catholicos of All Armenians sits at Etchmiadzin, with a second catholicosate of Cilicia (now in Antelias, Lebanon) and patriarchates in Jerusalem and Constantinople. Bound up with Armenian identity, it endured the Genocide of 1915–1923 and Soviet repression.
traditions/armenian-apostolic/distinctiv: Mesrop Mashtots' alphabet and fifth-century Bible translation
Christmas and Theophany celebrated together on 6 January
Unmixed wine in the Eucharist and the madagh (blessed offering)
traditions/armenian-apostolic/profile/au: Scripture, Tradition, the three ecumenical councils and the Armenian Fathers such as Gregory of Narek and Nerses Shnorhali.
traditions/armenian-apostolic/profile/sa: Restoration and deification of humanity through the incarnate Word, received in the life of the church.
Seven sacraments, with infant baptism, chrismation and communion given together.
traditions/armenian-apostolic/profile/es: Resurrection, Christ's return and judgment; commemoration of the dead.
traditions/armenian-apostolic/profile/go: Episcopal, led by the Catholicos of All Armenians in Etchmiadzin, with the Catholicosate of Cilicia and patriarchates of Jerusalem and Constantinople.
traditions/armenian-apostolic/profile/wo: The Armenian Divine Liturgy in Classical Armenian (Grabar), with distinctive chant (sharakan).
traditions/armenian-apostolic/profile/ca: Old Testament with deuterocanonical books; the 27-book New Testament (3 Corinthians was historically read in some periods).
traditions/armenian-apostolic/status: Active; c. 9 million members worldwide (estimates vary).
traditions/syriac-orthodox/summary: The Miaphysite church of the Patriarchate of Antioch, which separated from the Chalcedonian hierarchy after the deposition of Patriarch Severus (518). Its hierarchy was rebuilt by Jacob Baradaeus, hence the older name 'Jacobite'. Using West Syriac liturgy, it produced scholars such as Bar Hebraeus and has communities in Syria, Iraq, Turkey (Tur Abdin), the diaspora and India, where the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church is its largest body.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/distinctives/: West Syriac liturgy and Aramaic-language heritage
Theological legacy of Severus of Antioch and Philoxenus of Mabbug
Ancient monasteries of Tur Abdin (e.g. Mor Gabriel)
Large Indian branch (Jacobite Syrian Christian Church)
Survival through repeated massacres, including the Sayfo (1914–1918)
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/autho: Scripture, Tradition and the Syriac Fathers, with the first three ecumenical councils.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/salva: Salvation through the incarnate Word who unites humanity to God, appropriated through faith, repentance and sacramental life.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/sacra: Seven sacraments, with the Eucharist offered using leavened bread.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/escha: Resurrection, judgment and prayer for the departed.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/gover: Patriarch of Antioch and All the East (residing in Damascus), with a catholicos for India.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/worsh: The Liturgy of St James and many other anaphoras, in Syriac and vernacular languages.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/profile/canon: The Peshitta tradition, with deuterocanonical books; historically some smaller NT books came in later.
traditions/syriac-orthodox/status: Active; perhaps 2–4 million including the Indian Jacobite church (estimates vary).
traditions/malankara-orthodox/summary: An autocephalous church of the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, who trace their faith to the apostle Thomas. After the Coonan Cross Oath (1653) rejected Portuguese Latinisation, part of the community received West Syriac bishops from the Syriac Orthodox Church (from 1665). Disputes over the Antiochian patriarch's authority led to the establishment of the Catholicate of the East in India (1912); the Malankara Orthodox Church upholds its autocephaly, while the Jacobite faction remains under Antioch, and the Indian Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled on the dispute.
traditions/malankara-orthodox/distinctiv: Apostolic heritage of St Thomas in India
West Syriac liturgy, now mostly in Malayalam
Catholicos of the East seated at Kottayam (Devalokam)
Indian cultural forms in church life
Long-running property and authority dispute with the Jacobite faction
traditions/malankara-orthodox/profile/au: Scripture, Holy Tradition, the three ecumenical councils and the church's own 1934 constitution.
traditions/malankara-orthodox/profile/sa: Theosis through participation in Christ by faith, sacraments and the ascetic life.
Seven sacraments; infant baptism with chrismation and communion.
traditions/malankara-orthodox/profile/es: Resurrection, Christ's return and judgment; prayers for the departed.
traditions/malankara-orthodox/profile/go: Autocephalous, under the Catholicos of the East and Malankara Metropolitan with a Holy Synod and elected association.
traditions/malankara-orthodox/profile/wo: The West Syriac Liturgy of St James in Malayalam, Syriac and English.
traditions/malankara-orthodox/profile/ca: The Peshitta canon with deuterocanonical books.
traditions/church-of-the-east/summary: The church of Christians in the Persian (Sasanian) empire, organised under the Catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon at the Synod of 410 and later based in Baghdad. It did not accept the condemnation of Nestorius at Ephesus (431) and adopted a Dyophysite Christology indebted to Theodore of Mopsuestia (opponents called it 'Nestorian', a label it rejects). Between the seventh and fourteenth centuries it was geographically the most widespread church in the world, reaching China, Mongolia, Central Asia and India, before collapse under Timur and later schism (1552) divided it into the lines that became the Assyrian and Chaldean churches.
traditions/church-of-the-east/distinctiv: Dyophysite Christology following Theodore of Mopsuestia
East Syriac liturgy (Addai and Mari, one of the oldest anaphoras)
Missions along the Silk Road to China and Mongolia
School of Nisibis and translation of Greek learning into Syriac and Arabic
Centuries of life under Zoroastrian, Muslim and Mongol rulers
traditions/church-of-the-east/profile/au: Scripture (the Peshitta), the Fathers—especially Theodore of Mopsuestia—and the synods of the Persian church.
traditions/church-of-the-east/profile/sa: Christ as the second Adam restores humanity to immortality; salvation is participation in the 'new age' inaugurated by his resurrection.
'Mysteries' including baptism, Eucharist, ordination, the holy leaven (Malka) and sign of the cross; lists varied.
traditions/church-of-the-east/profile/es: Strong emphasis on the two ages: this mortal age and the coming age of incorruption.
traditions/church-of-the-east/profile/go: Catholicos-Patriarch with metropolitans across Asia, including 'exterior provinces' in India and China.
traditions/church-of-the-east/profile/wo: East Syriac rite with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari; no icons in many periods, but the cross was central.
traditions/church-of-the-east/profile/ca: The Peshitta, which originally lacked 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation.
traditions/church-of-the-east/status: Historical as a single body; divided after 1552 into lines continued by the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church.
traditions/assyrian-church-of-the-east/s: The principal continuation of the historic Church of the East, whose patriarchal line survived in the Hakkari mountains and, after the massacres of 1914–1918, moved into exile; the patriarchate is now based in Erbil, Iraq. A calendar dispute in 1964 produced the separate Ancient Church of the East. In 1994 Patriarch Dinkha IV and Pope John Paul II signed a Common Christological Declaration affirming shared faith in Christ, and in 2001 Rome recognised the validity of the Anaphora of Addai and Mari.
traditions/assyrian-church-of-the-east/d: Direct heir of the East Syriac Church of the East
Liturgy of Addai and Mari, sometimes without explicit words of institution
Theotokos not used historically; prefers 'Mother of Christ'
Strong Assyrian ethnic and linguistic identity (Neo-Aramaic)
Large diaspora in the US, Australia and Europe
traditions/assyrian-church-of-the-east/p: Scripture (Peshitta), the Fathers including Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius, and the synods of the Church of the East.
Restoration of humanity in Christ, the second Adam, received through baptism and the life of the church.
Traditionally seven mysteries including the holy leaven (Malka) and the sign of the cross.
Resurrection and the coming age of immortality, with prayers for the departed.
Catholicos-Patriarch (seated in Erbil since 2015) and Holy Synod; hereditary patriarchal succession was abandoned in 1976.
East Syriac rite in Classical Syriac and Neo-Aramaic; churches traditionally without images except the cross.
traditions/assyrian-church-of-the-east/s: Active; c. 400,000 members, mostly in Iraq, Iran, Syria and the diaspora.
